read.sections.0.heading.source: A place on a sea passage
read.sections.0.heading.back: A place on a sea route

read.sections.0.text.source: Melaka is a city on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, in today's Malaysia. It lies beside the Strait of Malacca, a narrow sea passage between the peninsula and the island of Sumatra. Ships sailing between East Asia and West Asia could pass through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was an important port ruled by a Malay sultanate. A port like this can bring local people, visiting traders, goods and ideas together. Location helps explain why traders stopped there. But geography alone does not tell us who held power, or how each community lived. Find the strait on the modern map before you look at the older map.
read.sections.0.text.back: Melaka is a city on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, in the country of Malaysia today. The city lies beside the Strait of Malacca, a narrow sea route between the peninsula and the island of Sumatra. Ships sailing between East Asia and West Asia could pass through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was an important port ruled by a Malay sultanate. A port like this can bring together local people, visiting traders, goods and ideas. Its location helps explain why traders stopped there. But geography alone does not tell us who held power, or how each community lived. Find the strait on the modern map before you look at the older map.
read.sections.0.text.note: The city keeps its name "Melaka"; the strait is "Selat Malaka", its usual Indonesian name (as KEY_TERMS keeps usual Indonesian spellings of real places). Indonesian learners may know the city as "Malaka" too. "Malay Peninsula" → "Semenanjung Malaya" ("Semenanjung Melayu" is also used).

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Melaka is a city in Malaysia. It is next to the Strait of Malacca. This strait is a narrow sea between two lands. Ships going between East and West Asia sailed through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was a Malay sultanate. A sultan ruled it. It was a busy port. Traders came with goods and ideas. The strait helps explain why ships stopped there. But it does not tell us who had power.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Melaka is a city in Malaysia. The city is next to the Strait of Malacca. This strait is a narrow sea between two lands. Ships going between East Asia and West Asia sailed through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was a Malay sultanate. A sultan held power there. Melaka was a busy port. Traders came bringing goods and ideas. The strait helps explain why ships stopped there. But the strait does not tell us who had power.

read.sections.1.heading.source: What a heritage record tells us

read.sections.1.text.source: UNESCO lists Melaka and George Town as World Heritage cities. It says they grew through more than 500 years of trade and exchange between East and West. It names Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures, and three European powers that ruled one after another. In 1511, Portuguese forces took Melaka. Dutch rule began in 1641, and British rule came later. The city changed over these periods. UNESCO's account is a modern heritage summary, not a diary kept by someone in Melaka in the 1400s. It helps us ask questions about long-term change. To hear one resident's view, we would need a source made closer to that person's life.
read.sections.1.text.back: UNESCO puts Melaka and George Town on the list of World Heritage cities. UNESCO says the two cities grew through more than 500 years of trade and exchange between East and West. UNESCO names Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures, and three European powers that ruled one after another. In 1511, Portuguese forces seized Melaka. Dutch rule began in 1641, and British rule came later. The city changed during these periods. UNESCO's description is a heritage summary from today, not a diary written by someone in Melaka in the 1400s. The description helps us ask about change over a long time. To hear one resident's point of view, we need a source made closer to that person's life.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: UNESCO says Melaka is a heritage city. People today care for its old places. UNESCO says people traded there for more than 500 years. UNESCO wrote this in modern times. It is not a diary from the 1400s.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: UNESCO says Melaka is a heritage city. People today look after its old places. UNESCO says people traded there for more than 500 years. Malay, Chinese and Indian people shaped the city. Europeans also held power there. In 1511, the Portuguese seized Melaka. In 1641, the Dutch seized it. Later, the British held power there. UNESCO wrote this in the present time. This is not a diary from the 1400s.

read.sections.2.heading.source: A map from a later time
read.sections.2.heading.back: A map from a later time

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a map of Melaka dated 1604, by a mapmaker named Manuel Godinho de Erédia. It comes from the Portuguese period, about 90 years after the Portuguese took the city. The map shows a large fort, a river and roads, with Portuguese labels. Some places around the fort have names, but we see few homes or people at work. A map shows what its maker chose to show, from his perspective. It is not a photo. So the map can help us study Melaka in the Portuguese period. It cannot show us what the sultanate's city looked like a century before.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a map of Melaka dated 1604, by a mapmaker named Manuel Godinho de Erédia. This map comes from the Portuguese period, about 90 years after the Portuguese seized the city. This map shows a large fort, a river and roads, with labels in Portuguese. Some places around the fort have names, but we see only a few houses or people at work. A map shows what its maker chose to show, from his point of view. A map is not a photo. So this map can help us study Melaka in the Portuguese period. This map cannot show what the sultanate's city looked like a century before.

watch.summary.source: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a TV company in Japan. It is about Melaka and George Town, two old cities by the Strait of Malacca. UNESCO's notes on the film say that people traded in the two cities for more than 500 years. Goods and ideas moved between East and West. People from Asia and Europe shaped the cities and left a mixed heritage. The notes say Melaka's old buildings show the early part of this history. UNESCO says this history began with the Malay sultanate in the 1400s. Then the Portuguese and the Dutch ruled, from the early 1500s. As you watch, remember that the film was made in our time. It shows buildings that are still standing, not people from the 1400s.

Evidence move: point to the date 1604 on the map and its caption before asking anything about the 15th-century sultanate. A sound answer says location helps explain a port, and that the later map has an explicit limit. Misconception to address: the map was not drawn during the sultanate, and a modern UNESCO summary and a 1604 map are two different kinds of source.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: Melaka was one of many ports in the region, so avoid suggesting it stands for all of Southeast Asia; and peoples named in a heritage summary did not share equal power. The date 1604 comes from the Commons file page and the brief. Erédia's book named in the file's credit line, the Declaraçam de Malaca, is usually dated about 1613; an NUS Press study says one of his strait maps in it is dated 1604 but does not date this city plan. Either way the map is from the Portuguese period, long after 1511.
